Copper Long-term Outlook 
Executive summary 
The global economy is continuing to shake off the effects of its worst recession since the end of World 
War II.  However, as far as copper demand is concerned the recovery has not been universal, with 
demand in several of the mature economies forecast to decline significantly in 2009.  This particularly 
applies to demand in Western Europe, the US and Japan where we estimate that consumption will 
decline this year by ~22%, 21% and 30% respectively.  In contrast demand in China is forecast to grow 
by a healthy 23% this year, partly offsetting the sharp declines in Western Europe, the US and Japan.  
Overall we forecast that global refined copper consumption will fall by 5.1% this year to 17.1Mt.   
During the current price cycle, which is projected to run from 2002 to 2009, we forecast that global 
copper consumption will grow at an average rate of 1.8% p.a. which is below the average annual 
growth rate in the previous price cycle which ran between 1993 and 2002.  The lower growth will reflect 
contracting demand in the mature economies, namely Western Europe, North America and Japan.  
Elsewhere strong growth in the Eastern Bloc is anticipated.   
We now expect base case mine production to increase by 1.5% during 2009 to ~15.8Mt, and production 
capability by 6.3% in 2010 to 16.8Mt.  Between 2002 and 2009 the average annual growth rate in base 
case world copper mine production capability (excluding highly probable and probable projects) is 
forecast to be just 1.8% p.a., including 1.4% p.a. ex-concentrates and 3.4% p.a from SxEw sources.   
Base case mine production capability is forecast to decline by 1% p.a. between 2009 (inclusive) and 
2020 with mine output falling from a peak of ~18.1Mt in 2012 to ~13.8Mt in 2020.  However, note that 
this rate of decline does exclude our anticipated mine disruption allowance (6% of initial mine 
production capability forecast) and any price related/market adjustment.  At the same time, demand for 
additional mine production (including the disruption allowance) to meet increased market requirements 
for refined metal will create an implied shortfall in mine output of ~0.3Mt/a in 2011, 5.6Mt/a in 2017 and 
9.9Mt/a by 2020. 
We now expect base case global copper smelter production to decline by 1% year on year to ~14.1Mt/a 
in 2009.  In terms of capacity this should increase by 2.6% in 2010 to 17.9Mt and by a further 4% in 
2011 to 18.6Mt.  During the forecast period global smelter production capability is expected to increase 
by 2.4% p.a., rising from 14.2Mt at the end of 2008 to just under 18.9Mt by 2020.   
Our forecast global market surplus for 2009 is ~1.2Mt which is significantly above our previous estimate 
of a 0.6Mt.  The higher surplus reflects steep downward corrections to a number of our demand 
forecast following our LME week discussions and subsequent conversations with copper producers and 
fabricators.  As a consequence, metal stocks, in terms of days of consumption, are forecast to reach 75 
days this year, up from our previous forecast of 65 days.  We now expect that cash prices in 2009 will 
average $5162/t ($2.34/lb), up 4.7% from our previous estimate of $4930/t ($2.25/lb).  The higher price 
reflects the stronger price environment witnessed during the quarter.

Overview 
Global economy beginning to stabilise  The global economy is continuing to shake off the effects of its worst 
recession since the end of World War II.  The concerted efforts of governments and central banks around the world have 
successfully stabilised the financial system and prevented the recession from developing into a depression.  However, as 
far as copper demand is concerned the recovery has not been universal, with demand in several of the mature 
economies forecast to decline significantly in 2009.  This particularly applies to demand in Western Europe, the US and 
Japan where we estimate that consumption will decline this year by ~22%, 21% and 30% respectively.  In contrast 
demand in China is forecast to grow by a healthy 23% this year, partly offsetting the sharp declines in Western Europe, 
the US and Japan.  Thus we forecast that global refined copper consumption will fall by 5.1% this year to 17.1Mt.   
Mature economy copper demand forecast to decline for the third consecutive year  Copper demand in the mature 
economies is forecast to decline by 22.7% this year to just below 5.4Mt, its lowest level, according to our records, which 
date back to 1976.  Given the severity of the downturn the recovery in copper consumption in the mature economies will 
be slow.  We expect that 2010 will be a transitional year with demand increasing more strongly in 2011.  Historically, 
strong first use copper demand growth has occurred 18 months to two years after the low-point in a recession-driven 
downturn in consumption.  This is because many applications for copper in, for example, the construction sector, tend to 
be required towards the end of construction projects (plumbing, wiring, decorative items).  Reflecting this, demand in the 
mature economies is forecast to recover by 2% in 2010, to just under 5.5Mt, before increasing by a more robust 5.8% in 
2011 to ~5.8Mt.  However, thereafter demand is expected to decline on an annual basis throughout the forecast period to 
2020.  The negative trend reflects the displacement of first-use demand away from the mature economies to the 
developing economies, especially in China, Mexico, and Vietnam.  In recent years there has been a growing trend of 
copper semis manufacturers moving their production facilities to areas where production costs (labour, environmental, 
power etc) are considerably lower.  Prime examples include Mexico and Vietnam where two of China’s largest copper 
tube producers have recently set up new copper tube mills: Golden Dragon in Mexico and Hailiang in Vietnam.  In 
addition, increased exports of competitively priced copper products from China, and other developing economies, into 
the mature economies will impact negatively on the production of copper semi products (from the mature economies) 
resulting in some production facilities becoming obsolete.  This is already beginning to occur within the wire rod market 
following the closure of Freeport’s Chicago plant at the end of last year and the forthcoming (official) closure of Nexan’s 
Chauny wire rod plant in France at the beginning of next year.  Reflecting these growing trends we have lowered 
significantly our long term first-use demand estimates for the mature economies since our previous Long Term Outlook 
report.  We now forecast that first-use demand in the mature economies will decline by 4% p.a. during the forecast 
period, falling from ~6.9Mt at the end of 2008 to ~4.2Mt in 2020  Previously we expected a decline of 2% p.a. with 
demand falling to ~5.3Mt by 2020. 
Healthy growth forecast in copper demand in the developing economies  In contrast, we have lifted our long term 
forecasts for the developing economies and now forecast that demand will grow by 5.9% this year, to 11.7Mt, and by 
7.9% and 7.4% in 2010 and 2011 to ~12.7Mt and 13.6Mt respectively.  The strong growth rates largely reflect robust 
Chinese demand which is expected to increase by 23% this year, 10% in 2010 and 8% in 2011 to ~6.3Mt, 6.9Mt and 
7.5Mt respectively.  This growth will be supported by continued investment within the power sector.  Further out demand 
will continue to improve on an annual basis where refined copper consumption within the developing economies is

forecast to increase by 5.8% p.a. between 2009 (inclusive) and 2020.  Thus refined copper consumption will rise from 
~11.1Mt at the end of 2008 to 21.8Mt by 2020.  This strong rate of growth will reflect healthy copper demand from China 
(+7.5% p.a), Africa (+5.9%p.a.), India (+9% p.a.), Vietnam (+9% p.a.), United Arab Emirates (+16.5% p.a.), Brazil (+6.2% 
p.a.) and Mexico (+4% p.a.).   
Long term global demand forecast is unchanged  Despite the amendments we have made to our demand forecasts 
in both the mature and developing economies, overall our long term global demand growth estimate of 3.1% p.a. 
between 2009 and 2010 is unchanged from our previous Long Term Outlook report.  In the near term, we forecast that 
global refined copper consumption will fall by 5.1% this year, to 17.1Mt, before recovering by 6% in 2010, to ~18.1Mt, 
and 6.9% in 2011 to just under 19.4Mt.   
Demand forecast to grow by 1.8% p.a. during the current price cycle  During the current price cycle, which is 
projected to run from 2002 to 2009, we forecast that global consumption will grow at an average rate of 1.8% p.a. (see 
table below) which is below the average annual growth rate in the previous price cycle which ran between 1993 and 
2002.  As noted previously the lower growth will reflect contracting demand in the mature economies, namely Western 
Europe, North America and Japan.  Elsewhere strong growth in the Eastern Bloc is anticipated.  This is particularly true 
of Russia and China where demand is forecast to rise at an average rate of 7.2% p.a. and 13.8% p.a. respectively.  In 
Russia the strong increase in refined copper consumption reflects firm production growth in the domestic production of 
copper wire rod while in China robust growth in the domestic output of both wire rod and copper semi products is 
responsible.  However, the removal of the Russian 5% export duty on cathodes earlier this year now means that the 
incentive to convert cathode into wire rod, which previously was exempt from export duties, has been removed.  This 
change in trade duties is reflected in our forecast of negative growth (-0.5% p.a.) in Russian refined copper consumption 
during the forecast period 2009-2020.   
 
China 
Robust Chinese demand despite collapse in export demand  The combination of government spending and readily 
available credit has provided enough fuel for the Chinese economy to overcome the collapse in export demand for 
Chinese goods.  The Chinese government’s $585Bn stimulus package together with a projected $1.46Tn in new bank 
lending has, according to the World Bank, accounted for 80% of China’s growth this year.  Spending on metal intensive 
areas such as railways construction, roads and public housing, has helped offset the negative impact that the collapse of 
export markets has had on Chinese copper demand.  
Rebound in China’s real estate sector  The Chinese surge in lending has re-invigorated the country’s real-estate 
sector with developers re-starting work on projects that were placed on hold at the end of last year as well as initiating a 
swathe of new projects in recent months.  The pace of house sales in Beijing reached a record high in November and 
growth will accelerate in the country’s smaller cities given the easing of residency restrictions that previously made it 
difficult for rural dwellers to buy property in cities.  However, the authorities are also reported to be considering measures 
to reduce the amount of borrowing by the country’s property developers.

Tax cuts provide boost to consumer goods demand  Other government measures, including tax cuts, have helped 
drive demand for consumer goods such as home appliances and cars.  The tax cut on small cars resulted in sales rising 
to above 12M units in the first 11 months of the year and seems set to exceed 13M units for the year as a whole, up from 
9.6M units in 2008.  Production, meanwhile, totalled 11.18M units in the first ten months of the year, a year on year rise 
of 35%.  Although it remains to be seen whether the tax cuts will be maintained next year, it seems unlikely that this 
years stellar growth rates will be maintained.  If the tax cut is extended the urgency to buy will be reduced which will 
result in a gentle slowdown in the pace of sales.  Alternatively, if the cut is eliminated, sales are likely to fall sharply.

Double-digit growth in the production of copper-intensive white goods  Meanwhile the success of the spending 
vouchers on white goods was noticeable in the latest data from the National Bureau of Statistics, which showed the 
production of refrigerators, freezers and computers rising annually by 16.7%, 17% and 21% respectively during the first 
ten months of the year.  It was also reported that producers of copper and copper alloy products believed that underlying 
demand had improved and, more importantly, this was not solely driven by the recent government subsidy programmes.  
An improvement in general living standards and strong orders from the construction sector were also reported to be 
responsible.  These conditions supported the 28% year on year increase in copper semis output in October, according to 
the National Bureau of Statistics.  For the year-to-date (Jan-Oct) output is up 17% from the corresponding period in 2008.  
Further increases are expected as new capacity continues to come on line.  Zhongse Albetter Albronze Co. recently 
announced that its new 30kt/a copper tube plant and 40kt/a copper plate and strip project were launched during this 
month on the 12th.  Prior to that Wenzhou Metals Co. commissioned its new 10kt/a copper rod project on the 7th.   
Expected recovery in China’s export markets in 2010  Next year, it seems that Chinese exports will once again start 
to make a positive contribution to Chinese growth.  According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF), exports 
contributed 30% of China’s GDP growth over the period 2001-2008; if investment in capacity linked to exports is 
included, this figure rises to 60%.  In the medium-term, at least, exports will remain important to Chinese copper 
consumption particularly in the form of copper semi products and copper-containing consumer goods.   
Robust growth in Chinese copper demand this year  We forecast that Chinese refined copper consumption will 
increase by 23% this year to just under 6.3Mt.  Supporting this growth is the impact of the stimulus package, readily 
available credit and ongoing investment within the power sector.  In 2010 the gradual recovery of export demand will 
outweigh any tightening in credit conditions and result in copper consumption growing by 10%  to 6.9Mt.  By 2011, we 
forecast that the dissipation of the impact of the stimulus package and this year’s surge in lending will be more than 
offset by strong demand for Chinese exports which will lift Chinese copper consumption by a further 8% to ~7.5Mt.  
Throughout the forecast period Chinese refined copper consumption is forecast to grow by 7.5% p.a., rising from 5.1Mt 
at the end of 2008 to 12.3Mt by 2020.

US auto sales may not reach 10M units in 2009  The automotive sector forms one of the keystones of the US 
manufacturing sector.  Therefore the fact that this year’s monthly peak in car and light vehicle production, of 668k units in 
October, is just 179k units above the 1986-2008 low and 30% below the monthly average, highlights the extent of the 
weakness in the US automotive sector.  Production of cars and light vehicles in the first 11 months of the year totalled 
5.2M units, a year on year decline of 37%.  With the cash for clunkers party being followed by a sales hangover, sales in 
November totalled just 747k units, a month-on-month decline of 11% and fractionally lower than the then unprecedented 
low reached in November 2008.  It is possible that total auto sales may not reach the 10M unit level this year following 
several new record lows being reached thus far this year.  If 10M units are not reached then this will be 30% below the 
levels reached in 2008 and well below the annual average figure of 16.8M units reached over the first seven years of this 
decade. 
No improvement in US construction sector  The US construction sector also remains desperately weak.  Worse still, 
the outlook for the more copper-intensive non-residential construction sector is expected to remain depressed through 
2010.  According to the American Institute of Architects, its October billings index improved markedly, climbing by 3 
points to 46.1.  However, while this latest reading is welcome, it would suggest that the US non-residential construction 
sector will remain weak for at least the first half of 2010 and probably until 2011 given the 5-12 month lead time between 
architectural billings and the actual start of construction.  Nevertheless, one potential source of hope for non-residential 
construction next year is the additional government spending on infrastructure.  Discussions are currently underway in 
Congress that could result in the release of $35Bn for ‘shovel ready’ projects in February next year.  Such investments, if 
approved, will be a major boost for both copper wire and cable and copper semi products.   
Sharp drop in US wire rod production  The extent of the slowdown in construction activity was highlighted by one 
major US wire rod producer who reported to us recently that production from his plant was expected to decline by 27% 
(~86kt) this year.  Unfortunately production from this plant is solely destined for the construction sector so no 
improvement is expected until construction activity recovers.  The wire rod producer believes that the residential sector 
has now hit bottom but the commercial sector still has further to fall.  He does not expect any recovery in demand for 
copper wire rod from the construction sector until H2 next year.  As a consequence of this his production of copper wire 
rod is expected to decline by a further 1-2% next year.  The sharp decline in wire rod production thus far this year was 
underlined further by the American Bureau of Metal Statistics who recently reported a 25% (-296kt) drop in the 
production of copper wire rod in the US during the first nine months of the year from the corresponding period in 2008.   
No recovery in copper tube market  The downturn in the US construction sector also continued to impact negatively on 
demand for copper tube.  Wolverine Tube, a major copper tube producer, reported a 25.4% drop in its shipments of 
copper tube during Q3 from a year earlier.  The decline reflected deteriorating demand from the HVAC (Heating 
Ventilation and Air Conditioner) and the electrical appliance markets.  However, on a slightly positive note, Wolverine 
Tube did report that some of its customers from the industrial HVAC were forecasting an increase in order levels next 
year.  Taking all of the above into account we forecast that US refined copper consumption will decline by 21.2% this 
year to just above 1.5Mt.   
Sharp fall in US demand for copper this year  We forecast that the demand for refined copper consumption in the US 
will drop by ~21% this year to just above 1.5Mt.  in 2010 a small recovery is expected, with demand increasing by 0.8% 
to ~1.6Mt.  However, in 2011 US refined copper consumption is forecast to increase by a much healthier 3.9%, to just 
over 1.6Mt, as consumer and business confidence improves and demand from the construction sector picks up.

Negative growth forecast for US copper demand during 2009-2020  Over the forecast period 2009-2020 we project 
that US demand for copper will decline by 3% p.a., reflecting structural changes in the global economy which will see 
manufacturing and semis capacity relocating to lower wage economies, such as Mexico and China.  There will also be 
an increase in the amount of demand satisfied by imports rather than domestic production.  By 2020 we forecast that 
North American consumption will total ~1.4Mt.  This will account for ~5.2% of the global total compared with ~11% in 
2008.   
 
 
Europe 
European manufacturing PMI clears 50  In Europe, the impact of the various stimulus packages deployed by the 
governments of the region have helped place the economy on the road to recovery.  The European Union purchasing 
manager’s index for October climbed above the 50 level for the first time since May 2008 while the services PMI reached 
50.28, the first time it has been above 50 since April 2008.  Meanwhile, the preliminary PMI estimates for the Eurozone 
suggest that the region’s manufacturing and services sector continued to expand.   
But strong euro could threaten pick up   While government measures have played the main role in stimulating the 
European economy, improving export demand is now starting to make a contribution, particularly in Germany.  European 
Union exports climbed in month on month terms by 21.9% in September; however, in year on year terms exports are still 
down by 18.4%.  While exports are improving, the appreciation of the euro against the US dollar, Yuan and most other 
major currencies means that European products are becoming less competitive and this threatens the revival in the 
sector. 
European auto sector reliant on exports  One sector that has become increasingly reliant on exports is the European 
automotive industry.  German car and light vehicle production increased year on year in October despite the end of the 
government-led incentive programme the previous month.  Output was 531k units, down from 534k units in September, 
but 6.9% higher than a year ago.  Sales increased by 18.9% year on year, to 342.2k units.  Some of the increase can be 
attributed to a general recovery in the economy, and also to incentives now being offered by VW and Ford, including 
interest-free credit and various rebates.  Year-to-date output totalled 4.2M units in the ten month period, 19.3% lower 
than the corresponding period in 2008.  Meanwhile total EU25 car sales totalled 1.23M units in October, 11.7% higher 
year on year, with sales in Western Europe 15.8% higher year on year.  The largest gain was in the UK, where car sales 
increased by 31.6% year on year reflecting the ongoing cash incentive programme.  According to automotive 
consultants, J D Power, car production for Western Europe totalled 9M units in the first ten months of the year, a year on 
year decline of 23%.  The automotive consultants estimate that production in Europe as a whole (including Russia, 
Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Turkey) totalled 13.1M units, a year on year decline of 19%. 
Despite improving signals from the auto and the manufacturing sector generally, European demand for copper remains 
extremely weak.  In France cathode demand has fallen sharply following the closure of Nexan’s Chauny wire rod plant 
since September 17th because of strike action.  Workers are objecting to the company’s decision to close the plant at the 
beginning of next year.  Our sources indicated that it is now very unlikely that the plant will re-open at all.  The company 
recently announced that its Lens wire rod plant will take up some of the lost production by increasing its capacity to a 5-
day shift, according to our sources.  By doing this the company is hoping to lift production from 165kt to 190-195kt.  
However, market sources believe that this ramp up in production is questionable because the plant has never operated 
at this rate before.  Instead, production is more likely to reach between 175-180kt, according to our sources.  Taking the 
wire rod plant closure into account we now forecast that French refined copper consumption will decline by 36.2% this 
year to ~240kt, and by a further 23.6% in 2010 to 185kt.   
Spanish copper demand down sharply  In Spain refined copper demand has fallen significantly during the year and is 
one of the worst affected European economies.  Deteriorating market conditions reflect the sharp contraction in 
construction activity.  As a consequence the relatively new La Farga wire rod plant (180kt/a) which came on stream last 
year is currently running at only 50%, according to our sources.  This is below the plant’s original plans of ramping 
production up to over 75% of capacity during the first three years of operation.  It was also reported that production from 
Spain’s other two wire rod plants, Cunext (180kt/a) and SIA (57kt/a), was struggling.  Reflecting this we forecast that 
Spain’s refined copper consumption will fall by 3.8% this year to 260kt.  Next year a small recovery is anticipated which 
will see demand increase by 0.8% to 262kt.   
German copper order levels improve in some areas  In Germany our sources informed us that Aurubis’s order levels 
fell by 50-55% during the first few months of the year.  This reflected heavy de-stocking by the company’s customers 
during this time.  However, our sources also informed us that since that time Aurubis’s order levels have recovered.  As a 
consequence the company is now running at a production capacity rate of between 65-70%.  Despite this improvement 
we still forecast a 26% decline in German refined copper consumption this year to ~1Mt as demand continues to be 
impacted by the downturn in the region’s construction and auto sectors.

Further deterioration in Italian demand for copper and copper alloy products  Demand for copper wire rod is also 
weak in Italy, reflecting deteriorating orders from the domestic construction sector.  It was also reported that financial 
issues are causing additional problems for one particular wire rod producer.  The continued slowdown in the construction 
sector is also continuing to hamper demand for copper and copper alloy products.  This was highlighted recently when 
Assomet, Italy’s Non-ferrous National Association, reported a significant decline in the production of copper bars and 
sections and copper tube during Q3 from a year earlier.  According to the Association, output of copper bars and 
sections declined by 95.5% year on year while the production of copper tube fell by 26.4%.  Copper products, overall, 
declined by 9.6%, to 122.8kt, while the output of copper and copper alloy products weakened by 26.4%, to 82.4kt, year 
on year through to September.  For the first nine months of the year the Association reported a 26.2% annual decline in 
the production of copper and copper alloy products to 685kt.  With this in mind we forecast a 22% decline in Italian 
refined copper consumption this year to ~500kt.   
Rising credit insurance costs may be an issue for European wire rod market next year  A major concern for the 
wire rod sector next year is rising credit insurance costs.  One wire rod producer explained that during the first two 
months of next year credit insurance for some wire rod producers is due to expire and they are unlikely to renew it 
because it is too expensive.  Credit insurance has risen in tandem with rising copper prices and, according to our 
sources, can add 5 euros/t to the overall price of the copper wire rod.  Nevertheless, in today’s uncertain market it is very 
difficult to trade without this.  Therefore, if producers do not have it then they will be pushing for much reduced payment 
terms or even cash in advance.  However, consumers will be looking for extended payment terms meaning that those 
producers without credit insurance could lose out on market share.  Thus next year could be a very difficult year for some 
wire rod producers with further closures a possibility.   
Weak outlook for European demand for copper semis products  European demand for copper and copper alloy 
products is also expected to remain weak next year.  KME, one of the region’s largest producers of copper and copper 
alloy products, recently reported that its output in 2010, while recovering from this year’s dire levels, will not reach the 
levels achieved in 2007 and 2008.  The company expects that production this year will fall by 30% from 2008, while 
recovering by 10-15% in 2010.  With this in mind we forecast that Western European demand for copper will fall by 
21.9% this year to just under 2.7Mt.  In 2010 we forecast a 2.5% gain in Western European refined consumption.  This 
may seem a bit high, in light of the weak outlook for next year; however the recovery will be coming from a low base and, 
at ~2.7Mt, demand will still only be equal to levels reached in 1987.   
European copper demand will trend lower during the forecast period  Throughout the forecast period 2009 to 2020 
Western European refined copper consumption growth is forecast to decline by 4.9% p.a.  Demand will fall from 3.4Mt in 
2008 to ~1.9Mt in 2020.  in term of the global total this will account for 7% which is down significantly from the share of 
19% at the end of 2008.  Likewise with the US, the contraction reflects increased cheaper imports from developing 
economies in Asia, including China, as well from Eastern Europe where labour and energy costs are much cheaper.  For 
the forecast period as whole, we expect that Western European demand will fall by 2.1% p.a, declining from 3.4mt in 
2008 to 2.6Mt in 2020.

Trends in consumption of secondary copper 
Scrap definition 
Copper scrap is classified into two general categories called old and new scrap.  New scrap, or manufacturing scrap, is 
generated during the fabrication of copper products and returned to the mill for reprocessing, or sold, and is not 
considered a new source of copper supply.  A manufacturer may generate up to 60% of scrap as clippings, trimmings, 
stampings, borings, and turnings when processing copper and copper-base products into finished articles.  New scrap is 
termed "run-around" or home scrap (which does not enter the scrap statistics) when it is generated internally at the plant 
re-using it, or it may be called "purchased return scrap" when returned by a customer from a plant external to that 
purchasing and re-using it.  Old scrap is generated from worn out, discarded or obsolete copper products and thus, is 
considered to be a “new” source of supply 
Scrapping rates 
The availability of old copper scrap is linked to the volume of copper-containing products installed/purchased and their 
life cycles, or duration.  The life of copper in electrical equipment and machinery averages 30-35 years; in non-electrical 
machinery, 15 years; in housing, 35-75 years; in transportation, 10 years; in all other sectors, about 10 years.  The 
average for the industry is estimated to be 15-20 years.  The rate of (old) scrap recovery and its availability to be the 
market is limited not only by copper's long life, but also by the sensitivity of scrap collection rates to market prices. 
Over the past 20 years, the volume of new copper scrap has not grown in line with industrial consumption of copper 
because manufacturing efficiencies have improved, leading to as much as a 50% fall in new scrap generation over the 
period. 
Scrap usage 
Most old scrap recovered from the market place must be reprocessed either by smelting and refining, or, to a lesser 
extent, by leaching and electrowinning to form a pure copper product.  Fire refining in a reverberatory or other furnace 
may be sufficient for the better grades of scrap.  This latter process uses oxidation, fluxing and reduction, with a refined 
ingot, wire bar, slab, or billet usually being the end product. 
Certain products, such as brass rod (manufactured using 80-90% scrap) can contain higher amounts of scrap than 
others while still maintaining product quality tolerance.  Others, such as wire rod, must contain far less impurities 
(typically 5%) since these could affect the drawability (leading to snapping) of the wire rod in producing wire.  New scrap 
is readily used by brass and copper tube mills to generate new semi-fabricated forms with little additional treatment.  
Because minimal clean-up procedures are needed, this type of scrap is commonly called "direct melt", or No.1 scrap.  In 
general, No. 1 scrap is contained in copper and copper-alloy products, rather than wire rod.  Scrap purchases by brass 
mills are based primarily on activity levels at the mills and the relative price differential between cathode and No. 1 scrap, 
rather than the actual copper price.  When business conditions are strong, brass mills have access to large volumes of 
return scrap.  When manufacturing (and, possibly imports) decline, mills may be forced to increase their cathode 
purchases. 
Low copper prices over the period 1997-2003 led to a reduction in the availability of smelting and refining grade scrap 
with a corresponding decline in the processing of this material in countries such the USA and in Europe.  The notable 
exception has been China where there has been an upward trend in the treatment of smelting and refining grade scrap 
material.  Economic and environmental considerations have also played a major role, with the cost of environmental 
compliance often leading to plant closures, particularly in the USA.  This is despite the fact that the cost of recovering 
one tonne of copper from scrap is approximately half that of recovery through the conventional route (concentrate-
smelting-refining).  Secondary smelters and ingot markers typically consume the lion's share (90%) of No.2 scrap and 
most of the auto radiators and red brass scrap. 
Scrap consumption 
During 2008 copper produced from scrap (at smelters, refineries and in direct use) was ~7.9Mt, representing 35% of total 
copper consumed.  Of all scrap consumed 59% went into direct use with smelting and refining absorbing 22% and 19% 
respectively.   
It can be seen from the chart below that copper produced from scrap has exceeded 37% of the total market (i.e. direct 
use scrap plus refined copper production) on only two occasions over the past 18 years, these being in 1990 and 1995.  
Between 1997 and 2003 there was a steady decline in overall scrap use, falling to a low of 29%, in 2003, before

Our long term copper price is not the same as our long term average price  Over the forecast period (2009-2020) 
we predict that prices will average $5638/t ($2.56/lb) in constant 2009$.  However, it is important to note that this is not 
our long-term price forecast because this period includes several years where prices are expected to be substantially 
above normal levels.  This is expected because of the general lack of greenfield and brownfield project capacity 
development in recent years and requirement for sufficient price encouragement to justify the development of additional 
mine capacity. 
Incentive pricing provides the most appropriate estimate of long-term average prices  For industries such as 
copper that are in structural deficit, that is with long-term demand significantly in excess of base case production 
intentions, we are of the opinion that while there are various techniques used by the industry to project long-term copper 
prices, incentive pricing provides the most appropriate estimate of long-term cycle average prices.   
The incentive price analysis examines the price required to provide an investor a given rate of return for each project, 
and calculates the price required in theory to warrant investment in sufficient cumulative capacity to meet potential 
demand.  In this context long-term can be considered the cycle average price over the next cycle, i.e. the decade over 
which a project would expect to see payback.   
Our project incentive price over the forecast period remains at $1.80/lb  In terms of long-term cycle average prices, 
these are critically dependant upon both the demand outlook and upon both capital and operating costs.  The incentive 
price methodology starts by estimating the demand for additional mine capacity after allowing for scrap usage and base 
case mine production changes.  Critically, in a demand growth scenario and one of depleting mines, the demand for 
additional capacity increases with time and care must be exercised in precisely defining the forecast period over which 
the cycle average price is to be estimated.  Capital costs have remained surprisingly resilient at elevated levels over 
2009 and the anticipated significant decline in input costs appears not yet to have materialised.  We therefore retain our 
view that, for the time being, an incentive price of around $1.80/lb remains reasonable over the period to 2020.  This said 
we are monitoring events in Chile with respect to water usage, and are in the process of quantifying the potential impact 
of the compulsory use of sea-water both on projects (should legislation move in this direction), and potentially on existing 
mines in the Atacama region.  An increase in operating costs of the order of 20c/lb and significantly higher capital costs 
could see the incentive price over the period to 2020 increase in excess of $2/lb.  Looking out beyond a decade, and 
factoring in the compulsory use of sea water, levels of $2.50/lb may not prove to be unreasonable.

Principle uses of copper 
Copper consumption can be divided into three main product groups which are copper wire rod, copper products and 
copper alloy products.  Copper wire rod, accounting for an estimated 53% of total Global consumption (i.e. including 
scrap) and 69.5% of primary consumption, is copper’s main first use.  With the exception of silver, copper has the highest 
electrical conductivity of all the metals.  This helps to explain why the principal application for copper wire rod is wire and 
cable.  Wire rod is consumed in five main wire and cable markets which include general and industrial cable, utility power 
cable, telecommunication cable, other insulated wire and winding wire.   
In general, wire and cable and copper products are consumed in five broad sectors: construction, electric and electronic 
products, industrial machinery and equipment, transportation equipment and consumer and general products.  Of these, 
construction is the largest sector for consuming copper, accounting for 32 of total copper consumption.  The main wire 
and cable and copper products consumed in the construction industry include building wire, power cable, copper 
plumbing and air conditioning tube, copper sheet and alloy products.   
Building wire is the largest of the wire and cable markets, accounting for ~35% of wire rod consumption.  Rising intensity 
of use, in both the mature and developing economies, will be largely responsible for building wire maintaining this 
position.  The number of electrical appliances used at home and at the workplace continues to rise, particularly in the 
mature economies, thereby leading to an increase in the number of power outlets needed per building.  In addition, 
recent technical issues imply that more copper wire and cable will be needed in the future.  One of these issues, 
electrical energy efficiency involves using less power to perform a given task by using more or heavier copper 
conductors.  Finally, good power quality, defined as the uninterrupted, undistorted flow of electricity at the correct 
voltage, is also helping to drive up the demand for building wire due to higher power quality being achieved by installing 
additional circuits and heavier wires and cables. 
In contrast to the building and industrial cable market, the power utility market is the smallest of all the wire and cable 
segments.  However, demand growth for power cable will be supported by both the general recovery in utility investment 
and the fact that copper, the mainstay of power grids worldwide, still has considerable potential to carry energy better 
and reduce losses than aluminium. 
Copper tube, accounting for an estimated 15% of global refined copper consumption in 2007, is the largest of the copper 
product markets.  The two main uses are in plumbing and heating systems and in air conditioners and refrigeration (ACR 
tube).  The steady proliferation of plumbing amenities in and around the home, particularly as many houses built today 
within the mature economies have more than one bathroom, are largely responsible for copper plumbing tube demand 
growth.  Elsewhere, improved living standards in the developing economies, leading to higher demand for air 
conditioners, continues to boost demand for ACR tube.  This is particularly the case in China and India where improved 
power supply will lead to a surge in the consumption of air conditioners over the coming years.  In 2007 China produced 
almost 80M units of (inexpensive) air conditioners which is significantly higher than the ~25M units produced in 2001.  
Meanwhile in the mature economies, the market is being driven by external factors such as environmental issues, 
regulatory concerns and social demands for comfort.   
Other copper and copper alloy products consumed by the construction sector include copper sheet and strip, rods, bars 
and sections plus brass products.  Copper sheet is used for roofing, eaves gutters, drain pipes for rainwater and lining for 
facades, while rods bars and sections, along with brass products, are used for building fixture and fittings.  In hospitals, 
brass doorknobs and push plates are widely used because it has been proven that they help to reduce cross 
contamination.   
Electrical and electronic products are copper’s second largest consuming sector, accounting for 32% of total copper 
demand.  Copper containing electrical and electronic products include telecommunication cable, power cable, 
transformer windings, semiconductors and motors for heavy appliances.  
Since the early 1990s copper telecommunication cable has been largely substituted by fibre optic cable in long distance 
networks.  However, owing to its high cost, copper telecom cable has remained the preferred link between the main 
network and consumers.  In addition, the development of the internet and e-mail has further enhanced the role of copper 
in telecommunications in recent years.  The need for information to be carried quicker along the telecommunication 
network has led to the introduction of asymmetrical digital subscriber line technology (ADSL).  The ADSL is a dedicated 
circuit between a home and the telephone company’s central office that uses normal copper telephone lines.  The 
addition of an ADSL chip to the existing copper network means that users can download files around 15 times faster than 
an analogue dial-up connection.   
There is also the potential for dramatic gains in copper consumption to occur within the home because of a system 
known to the telecommunications industry as ‘structured wiring’.  The cable carrying voice, computer and television 
signals is connected to a central hub in the home.  Individual cables then run independently from here to high-quality 
connections in rooms throughout the house.  Cables connected to the hub consist of four pairs of twisted wires, capable

The other main wire and cable segment to supply the electrical sector is winding wire.  In 2007 winding wire demand 
accounted for an estimated ~20% of copper wire rod consumption, making it the third largest wire and cable market.  
Applications include transformers, generators, stereos, television sets and motors.  Indeed, it is the need to improve 
electrical efficiency of this last application, particularly in the mature economies, that has generated the most growth in 
winding wire demand recently.  This is because improved electrical efficiency involves using a larger conductor in order 
to reduce electrical resistance, as well as ensuring that the proper voltages are delivered when needed.  In addition, the 
efficiency of electric motors is being improved further by introducing copper into the rotor as opposed to aluminium.  
Meanwhile, in the developing economies, demand growth will mainly stem from increased consumption of electrical 
goods as disposable incomes rise.   
Copper’s third largest consuming sector, industrial machinery and equipment, accounts for 12% of total consumption.  
Both copper wire and cable and semi products supply this sector which includes equipment and machinery, industrial 
valves and fittings, off-highway vehicles and heat exchangers.  Copper wire and copper and copper alloy products are 
also used in transportation equipment, copper’s fourth largest category.  This includes the automotive, marine and 
aircraft/aerospace sectors.  It is within the automotive sector that developments of new copper applications have been 
most concentrated in recent years.  Prior to 1930 copper and brass, having excellent pressure containing and anti-
corrosion characteristics, were the favoured materials to be used in brake tubing.  However, mass auto production in the 
1940s led to the adoption of furnace-brazed steel tubing because it was much lower in cost.  Although this form of tubing 
is still widely used today, copper has re-gained some of its lost market share through the introduction of a copper-nickel 
alloy (90% copper/10% nickel) which is more resistant to corrosion from road mud and salt than steel piping.  Likewise, 
new technology has led to the development of a new brazed copper-brass automotive radiator which has the necessary 
requirements to recapture some of the market share displaced by aluminium over the past twenty years. 
Meanwhile, 42-volt systems, hybrid vehicles and numerous electrical and electronic applications provide additional 
growth prospects for the use of copper within the automotive sector Over the years the number of electrical and 
electronic components installed per unit has been rising steadily, thereby creating the need for growth in the power and 
signal distribution system (otherwise known as the wiring harness).  Many of the electrical components will have to be 
redesigned in order to work effectively with the higher-voltage systems which could result in the copper content of some 
of the electrical components falling, but as more power becomes available, new electrical components will emerge.  Such 
examples include electronic valve actuation and electric braking, resulting in several kilos of copper, per unit, being 
added.  Forecasts have shown that over the next ten years, increases per vehicle will outweigh the decreases in copper 
required per component.  
Copper’s final end-use category is consumer and general products.  Copper consumed in this sector accounts for 10% of 
total copper consumption.  The three main end-uses are electrical appliances, military ordnance and coinage.  The 
production of the new Euro coin in recent years has helped to support demand for copper and copper alloy products.

Industrial Production Outlook 
The recovery in the global industrial economy has gathered momentum through the fourth quarter of 2009, as the 
significant fiscal and monetary stimulus packages of numerous governments, as well as the inventory cycle, lend a 
significant boost to industrial production.  However, like the financial crisis of late 2008 and subsequent fallout had the 
greatest effect on those economies that were most exposed to the global financial system, the emerging recovery from 
the collapse in output is progressing quicker in those economies which had less exposure. This has given rise to a 
pattern of winners and losers.  
The recovery in China, India, Brazil and South Korea has been remarkably robust, and industrial production growth in 
these economies is expected to return to trend levels in early 2010.  However, we do still have some concerns about the 
quality of recovery in these economies.  On the other end of the spectrum, the recovery in the more developed 
economies of Europe, the USA and Japan has been much more subdued, and there remain a number of key issues 
looming that could yet cause the recovery to falter.  
The key risks to the global economic recovery centre on the withdrawal of fiscal and monetary stimulus policies.  Almost 
without exception, the recoveries we have seen in the world’s major industrial economies, from the underperforming 
ones of Europe, the USA and Japan, to the powerhouses of Asia, are largely due to unprecedented and significant 
stimulus measures.  On the whole, these policies have been largely successful.  However, governments cannot afford to 
take on the burdens of the consumer and private investor indefinitely, and thus fiscal stimulus measures are expected to 
dry up into the second half of 2010.  Also, the ultra-loose monetary policy and quantitative easing employed by numerous 
major economies will need to be withdrawn to avoid a rapid rise in inflation. Authorities face a delicate balancing act 
between fuelling inflation, and withdrawing the monetary stimuli too soon, halting the recovery in its tracks. Wood 
Mackenzie believes that the chances are greater of a withdrawal too late, rather than too soon. 
On the whole, Wood Mackenzie has not made significant changes to its industrial production forecasts.  There have 
been downward revisions to 2009 numbers for some countries such as the USA and Japan, as a result of a more 
protracted inventory destocking cycle than we had previously expected.  Subsequently, the 2010 forecasts have been 
upwardly adjusted to take into account the lower 2009 base.  The outlooks for those economies worse affected by the 
financial crisis have been tempered, reflecting our view that their recovery will be protracted. On the other hand, we have 
increased our medium term forecasts for economies like those of Brazil, South Korea and India, who have demonstrated 
a greater resilience to the global recession.
